'''Otuke''' (Otuque, Otuqui) is an extinct language of the [[Bororoan languages|Bororoan language family]], formerly spoken in Brazil and Bolivia. Its closest relatives, the [[Kovareka language|Kovareka]] (Covareca) and [[Kuruminaka language|Kuruminaka]] (Curuminaca) languages, both extinct and poorly known, have sometimes been considered dialects of it.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=de CRÉQUI-MONTFORT |first=G. |last2=Rivet |first2=P. |date=1912 |title=Linguistique Bolivienne: Le Groupe Otukè |url=https://etnolinguistica.wdfiles.com/local--files/biblio%3Acrequi-montfort-rivet-1912-otuke/crequi-montfort_rivet_1912_otuke.pdf |journal=Journal de la Société des américanistes |volume=9 |pages=317–337 |issn=0037-9174}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=de CRÉQUI-MONTFORT |first=G. |last2=Rivet |first2=P. |date=1913 |title=Linguistique Bolivienne. Les Affinités Des Dialectes Otukè |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/44387220 |journal=Journal de la Société des américanistes |volume=10 |pages=369–377 |issn=0037-9174}}</ref>

== History ==
The name ''Otuqui'' was first mentioned in a 1726 book by Jesuit priest {{Interlanguage link|Juan Patricio Fernández|wikidata|Q19448042}}, listing the names of various [[Ranchería|rancherías]] in the region inhabitedd by the [[Chiquitano|Chiquito (Chiquitano) people]], including the ranchería of ''Otuquimaaca''. However, the connection with the Otuke people and language is unclear. A more evident connection to Otuke was made by [[Lorenzo Hervás]]'s 1784 book ''Catalogo delle lingue conosciute''. In 1838, [[Georg Ludwig Kriegk]] also mentioned the [[Otuquis Province]] in his book ''Das Land Otuquis in Bolivia'' based on reports by its secretary at the time, Moritz Bach. An extract in the [[Chiquitano language]] of the region was also given, which Kriegk thought incorrectly to be an attestation of Otuke.<ref name=":0">{{Cite thesis |date=2024-03-28 |title=Otuke: reviewing the only remaining data on an extinct Bolivian language |url=https://studenttheses.universiteitleiden.nl/handle/1887/3763735 |language=en |archive-url=http://web.archive.org/web/20241219064848/https://studenttheses.universiteitleiden.nl/handle/1887/3763735 |archive-date=2024-12-19|degree=MA|last=Mulder|first=Sophie|publisher=Universiteit Leiden}}</ref>

=== Documentation ===
The only contemporaneous documentation of Otuke was done by [[Alcide d'Orbigny]] between 1830 and 1833. At the time of his visit, the Otukes lived in the Jesuit mission of [[Santo Corazón]], one of the [[Jesuit Missions of Chiquitos]]. By then, only two elderly people could speak the original Otuke language, and the rest had all switched to Chiquitano.<ref name=":0" />

== Name ==
Combès (2012) suggests that -''toki'' ~ -''tuki'' ~ -''tuke'' (also present in the ethynonym ''[[Gorgotoqui language|Gorgotoqui]]'') is likely related to the [[Bororo language|Bororo]] animate plural suffix -''doge'' (i.e., used to form plural nouns for ethnic groups). Hence, the name ''Otuqui'' (''Otuke'') was likely etymologically related to the name ''[[Gorgotoqui language|Gorgotoqui]]''.<ref name="Combes-2012">Combès, Isabelle. 2012. Susnik y los gorgotoquis. Efervescencia étnica en la Chiquitania (Oriente boliviano), p. 201–220. ''Indiana'', v. 29. Berlín. {{doi|10.18441/ind.v29i0.201-220 }}</reF>

==Classification==
d'Orbigny compared his vocabulary of Otuke with those of the [[Saraveca language|Saraveca]] and Chiquitano languages, finding that they hardly had any similarities, though the minuscule vocabularies collected of Kovareka and Kuruminaka were similar. The first to propose a relationship between Otuke and Bororo was [[Karl von den Steinen]] (1895).<ref name=":0" /> Several attested extinct Bororoan varieties were either dialects of Otuke or closely related:<ref name="Loukotka">{{cite book |last=Loukotka |first=Čestmír |authorlink=Čestmír Loukotka |title=Classification of South American Indian languages |url=https://archive.org/details/classificationof0007louk |url-access=registration |publisher=UCLA Latin American Center |year=1968 |location=Los Angeles}}</ref><ref>{{Citation |last=Campbell |first=Lyle |title=Indigenous Languages of South America |date=2024-06-25 |work=The Indigenous Languages of the Americas |pages=198 |url=https://academic.oup.com/book/57386/chapter/464719092 |access-date=2025-05-21 |edition=1 |publisher=Oxford University PressNew York |language=en |doi=10.1093/oso/9780197673461.003.0004 |isbn=978-0-19-767346-1|url-access=subscription }}</ref>
*[[Covareca language|Covareca]] - [[Santa Ana de Velasco|Santa Ana]] mission, Bolivia
*[[Kuruminaka language|Curuminaca]] - Casalvasco mission, Bolivia
*Coraveca (Curave, Ecorabe) - [[Santo Corazón]] mission, Bolivia (unattested)
*Curucaneca (Curucane, Carruacane) - [[San Rafael de Velasco|San Rafael]] mission, Bolivia (unattested)
*Tapii - [[Santiago de Chiquitos]] mission, Bolivia (possibly [[Zamucoan languages|Zamucoan]])<ref name="Mason-1950">{{cite book |last=Mason |first=John Alden |authorlink=John Alden Mason |date=1950 |chapter=The languages of South America |editor-first1=Julian |editor-last1=Steward |title=Handbook of South American Indians |volume=6 |pages=157–317 |publisher=[[Smithsonian Institution]], [[Bureau of American Ethnology]] Bulletin 143 |location=Washington, D.C., Government Printing Office}}</ref>

[[Chiquitano language|Chiquitano]] speakers also lived in many of the missions.<ref name="Loukotka"/> All of the peoples listed above switched to Chiquitano by the 19th century.<ref>Handbook of South American Indians, vol. 3</ref>

(See [[Jesuit Missions of Chiquitos]] for locations.)

Mason (1950) says the first four are "separate and very different", but Loukotka (1968) notes that nothing is known of Curave or Curucane (or of Tapii), that only 14 words of Curumina and 19 of Covare have been preserved.<ref name="Loukotka">{{cite book |last=Loukotka |first=Čestmír |authorlink=Čestmír Loukotka |title=Classification of South American Indian languages |url=https://archive.org/details/classificationof0007louk |url-access=registration |publisher=UCLA Latin American Center |year=1968 |location=Los Angeles}}</ref>

== Grammar ==
The suffix {{Lang|mis|-ra}} is found in body part names. Similarly, the suffix {{Lang|mis|-ka}} is found on words for round fruits.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=de Créqui-Montfort |first1=Georges |last2=Rivet |first2=Paul |date=1912 |title=Linguistique Bolivienne: Le groupe Otuké |url=https://etnolinguistica.wdfiles.com/local--files/biblio%3Acrequi-montfort-rivet-1912-otuke/crequi-montfort_rivet_1912_otuke.pdf |journal=Journal de la Société des Américanistes |volume=IX |pages=317–352}}</ref>
